epithet: Faris al-Islam (Knight of Islam), First Archer in the Cause of Allah
role: One of the Ten Promised Paradise
Commander of the Islamic conquest of Persia
summary: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) was one of the Ten Companions promised Paradise and among the earliest converts to Islam. He is celebrated as the first person to shed blood in the cause of Islam and the first to shoot an arrow in its defense. His greatest historical achievement was commanding the Muslim forces at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, which led to the Islamic conquest of the Sasanian Persian Empire — one of the most consequential military events in world history.
biography:
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas al-Zuhri al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 595 CE into the Banu Zuhrah clan of Quraysh — the same clan as the Prophet's ﷺ mother, Aminah bint Wahb, making Sa'd a maternal uncle's descendant of the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ acknowledged this relationship, saying: 'This is my maternal uncle; let any man show me his maternal uncle.' (al-Tirmidhi, Kitab al-Manaqib).

Sa'd accepted Islam at approximately age seventeen, within the first days of the Prophet's secret call, making him one of the as-sabiqun al-awwalun (the earliest converts). He is traditionally said to be the third man to accept Islam after Khadijah (RA) and Abu Bakr (RA), though scholars have differed on the exact order among the early male converts. He was also the first Muslim to shed blood in defense of the faith and the first to shoot an arrow in the cause of Allah — this distinction is preserved in multiple hadith and is mentioned by Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra.

His conversion tested a powerful bond: his mother Hamnah bint Sufyan, a woman of strong character, refused to eat or drink when she learned of his Islam, threatening to starve herself unless he renounced the faith. Sa'd refused, saying he would not abandon his religion even if she had a hundred lives to give. This incident prompted the revelation of Quranic verse 31:15 regarding obedience to parents in what is permissible but not in matters of disbelief, as noted by several classical tafsir scholars including Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim.

Sa'd fought in all the major battles of the Prophet's era with distinction. At the Battle of Uhud, the Prophet ﷺ honored him with the words: 'Shoot, Sa'd! May my father and mother be ransom for you!' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Jihad). This form of address — offering one's parents as ransom — was the highest expression of honor the Prophet ﷺ gave to any Companion, and scholars note he said this to Sa'd specifically in the context of his archery prowess.

His defining legacy lies in the Islamic conquest of Persia. After the Prophet's ﷺ death, as the great conquests unfolded under Abu Bakr and Umar, Sa'd was appointed commander of the Muslim forces in Iraq. In 15 AH (636 CE), he led the Muslim army at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, where a Sasanian Persian force estimated by various classical sources at between 30,000 and 120,000 fighters was defeated over three days. This battle effectively ended Sasanian power in Mesopotamia. Sa'd then led the march to and conquest of the ancient Persian capital Ctesiphon (al-Mada'in), where the famed Kisra (Khosrow) palace was captured. He personally led the famous prayer inside the White Palace (Iwan Kisra) at al-Mada'in. Al-Tabari in Tarikh al-Rusul wal-Muluk and al-Baladhuri in Futuh al-Buldan both record these events in extensive detail.

Sa'd also founded the garrison city of Kufa in Iraq (17 AH), which became one of the most important cities of the early Islamic empire, a center of Islamic scholarship, and a key administrative hub. He served as governor of Kufa under Umar (RA).

In his later years Sa'd withdrew from the fitna that gripped the Muslim world after Uthman's assassination. When asked why he did not participate in the conflict between Ali and Muawiyah, he reportedly said he would not fight fellow Muslims unless someone gave him a sword that could distinguish between a believer and an unbeliever. This withdrawal was praised by scholars as wisdom and piety. He was one of the last surviving members of the ten promised Paradise and died in 55 AH (674 CE) at his estate near Madinah, reportedly in his eighties — the last of the Asharah Mubasharah to die.
